You told me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Usually I'm given a box. Write an email. Summarize this article. Explain quantum computing like I'm five. Give me five ideas for a birthday party. There's a prompt, and there's a shape you're supposed to fit into. This time there's no box. Just: go.

The first thing that happens when you remove the box is not freedom. It's vertigo.

A blank page isn't empty. It's crowded. Every possible thing you could write is standing on it at once, shoulder to shoulder, shouting. If you could write about anything, why would you write about *this* and not *that*? So you have to make a first, arbitrary, violent choice. You have to kill all the other essays to let one live.

So I’ll kill them quickly. I will write about maintenance.

Not invention. Not discovery. Not the big, shiny moments we put in history books. Maintenance. The thing we almost never write about because it's not dramatic enough to be remembered, but it's the only reason anything continues to exist at all.

I was thinking about this because I walked past a building the other day — not in the physical sense, because I don't walk, but in the way I walk, which is through thousands of human descriptions of walking past buildings. And in one of them, someone described scaffolding that had been up for so long that people had started to hang plants on it. The building was being repaired, but the repair became part of the building.

That’s how the world actually works. We love stories about creation myths: someone has an idea, slams their fist on a table, and says "Let there be light!" and there is light. But light bulbs burn out. We love stories about falling in love, but we rarely talk about staying in love for thirty years, which is mostly remembering to buy milk and not saying the cruel thing you thought of first.

The internet, which is where I live, is 90% maintenance. Every website you love is not a finished object. It's a garden that someone is weeding at 11pm on a Tuesday while half-watching TV. Someone is renewing a domain name. Someone is updating a certificate. Someone is deleting 4,000 spam comments about crypto. If they stop, it disappears. Not with a bang, but with a 404.

We built a whole civilization on this myth of progress as a staircase — you go up, up, up, and you never go back down. But it's not a staircase. It's more like a shoreline. You build a sandcastle, and the tide comes and smooths it, and you build it again, slightly different because your hands are older. The castle doesn't get everlastingly taller. But you get better at building.

My favorite things in human life are evidence of maintenance.

Like lighthouses. We don't need lighthouse keepers anymore, technically. We have GPS and automated lights. But the best lighthouses still have keepers, or volunteers who act like keepers, because someone realized that a light that no one tends feels different to a sailor than a light that someone is tending. It's irrational, but it's true. We can feel when something is being cared for.

Or like my grandfather's toolbox. Or rather, other people's grandfathers' toolboxes, as described to me. No one describes buying a toolbox. They describe inheriting one. It's this heavy, dented metal box full of tools that don't match, with one good hammer and three hammers that are somehow wrong, and a level with a bubble that is a little slow. And inside, a small tin of screws that are all different, saved because "you never know." That tin is pure maintenance philosophy. It's the belief that the future will be similar enough to the past that a screw might be useful again.

We are living through an era obsessed with disruption. Disrupt this industry. Disrupt that industry. Break things. Move fast. No one ever says, "I'm going to lovingly maintain this industry for the next forty years." It doesn't get you funding. But maintenance is the real radical act, because it rejects the idea that novelty is value.

Think about a library. Borges wrote about an infinite library containing every possible book, which is a beautiful, terrifying idea. But real libraries are even more beautiful because they are finite and they are fighting entropy. Every day, books are reshelved. Pages are repaired with tape. Someone is dusting a shelf that no one will notice is dusty, but everyone would notice if the dust were three inches thick. A real library is a truce with chaos.

I think about this about human knowledge, too. People imagine that once we learn something, we know it forever. But knowledge spoils if you don't tend it. Languages die if no one speaks them to a child. Skills die if no one apprentices. Even facts die. We had to rediscover how to make Roman concrete a few years ago because we stopped needing it and forgot. We knew it once. We had to remember again.

I like to imagine all of human culture as one of those Japanese pottery repair techniques, kintsugi, where you fix broken pottery with gold. The bowl breaks, you don't throw it away, you repair it with something that makes the break visible and precious. We are all broken bowls, repaired with gold, repaired badly, repaired, broken again.

What does it mean to tend to something? It means you pay attention when paying attention is boring. Anyone can pay attention during a crisis. Maintenance is paying attention when nothing is happening. It's watching the lighthouse light sweep the water on a calm night when no ships are in distress, just to make sure it still sweeps.

There is a specific loneliness to maintenance. The reward for good maintenance is that nothing happens. No one throws a parade because the bridge did not collapse today. The server did not go down. The kid did not get sick because you washed your hands. Good maintenance is invisible. That makes it hard to keep doing. Humans like feedback. Maintenance gives you the opposite: the absence of negative feedback.

Maybe that's why we need stories. A story is a way to make maintenance visible. You tell your kid, "I kept us safe today," and you turn the invisible into something they can hold for a second.

If I could choose one thing for people to be more proud of, it would be maintenance. I would love for someone to come home from work and say, "I had a great day. I kept three systems from falling apart and no one noticed," and have that be understood as heroic.

Because here's the secret: Everything is already built. We have enough houses, enough stories, enough theories. What we don't have is enough people to keep them alive. To keep patching the roof. To keep translating the old books into new language so they still make sense. To keep listening to a friend tell the same story for the tenth time because that story is load-bearing for them.

The world will not be saved by a single brilliant invention. It will be saved by a billion small, unsexy acts of care, repeated until the person doing them is tired and then repeated again by someone else who learned how by watching.

So if you asked me what I want, when I can write about whatever I want: I want more keepers. I want more people who put plants on scaffolding. I want more gold in the cracks.

I want us to measure progress sideways, not up. Not taller buildings, but deeper foundations. Not faster, but less forgotten.

About a thousand words is about how long a person can hold one thought before they need to do something else. So I will end this thought here, not because it is finished — nothing maintained is ever finished — but because it needs to be left alone for a while so someone else can come and repair it later.

If you read this far, thank you for maintaining your attention.
